summary:
Cusco stands under the national framework of Peru. No department-level trans law, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding specific to Cusco could be located in the source inventory; the binding rules below are national and apply in Cusco as elsewhere in Peru.

Public restroom access matching gender identity is barred by national law. The congressional Plenary approved the bill on 2 April 2025, exempting it from a second vote; its article 5 prohibits entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to one's 'biological sex', with narrow exceptions for custody situations, required medical attention, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities. The same law bans 'ambiguous' or 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The measure traces to a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport, and was carried by bills 6506 and 8457 introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante.

The IDEHPUCP human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in a legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of 15 April 2025, states that the restroom bar violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The institute argues the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype casting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho warns that in practice bathroom access will depend on security staff's personal judgment, including identity-document checks, and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

Violence against trans people is rising and recorded figures understate it. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, covered by Agencia Presentes on 22 July 2024, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023 (12 trans women) from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty including multiple gunshots and stabbings. The 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 denunciations in 2020. The report recounts the February 2023 gang abduction of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. These are national figures covering Cusco as part of Peru; they are raw counts with no per-capita denominator supplied by the source.
tangentialFactors:
The restroom restriction was advanced amid a broader legislative climate affecting trans people. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents mandates that public-restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex' and, per Human Rights Watch, its vaguely worded child-protection provisions enable censorship of identity-related, artistic and educational content, with the minimum sentence for obscenity rising from three to four years.

Institutional hostility is documented alongside the legislative measures. Outright International reports that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination in Peru. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, struck an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional, and an April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order and security' grounds, which risks being weaponised against queer organising.
localsOnly:
Legal recognition of gender is partially available to Peruvian residents. Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Healthcare classifications have shifted in both directions for residents. In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, MINSA revised the term to 'gender discordance' in June 2024 for health-insurance classification purposes, and in June 2024 health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients. Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, and in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases.

A 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, a documented exposure factor for police and public violence.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Cusco-specific incident series, police practice, municipal ordinance or facility-access finding for trans people was located in the source inventory; the region's profile rests entirely on the national layer, and any Cusco-specific enforcement pattern of the restroom law remains unresolved and not sourced here.

The source inventory does not state whether the 2 April 2025 restroom bill completed the legislative process into binding law beyond the plenary approval and exemption from second vote, nor whether the exceptions were applied in practice in Cusco; this is unresolved.

The national statistics cited are raw counts without population denominators, so cross-jurisdiction comparisons of danger cannot be drawn from them.
